claim: HIF-2α is essential for carotid body development and function.
source: HIF-2α is essential for carotid body development and function
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing loss of glomus cells in TH-HIF-2αKO mice and impaired physiological responses.

claim: There is an absolute developmental requirement for HIF-2α for growth and survival of oxygen sensitive glomus cells of the carotid body.
source: We show here that there is an absolute developmental requirement for HIF-2α, one of the HIF isoforms, for growth and survival of oxygen sensitive glomus cells of the carotid body.
evidence: Supported by histological data showing absence of glomus cells in TH-HIF-2αKO mice and increased TUNEL+ cells during development.

claim: The loss of glomus cells renders mice incapable of ventilatory responses to hypoxia.
source: The loss of these cells renders mice incapable of ventilatory responses to hypoxia, and this has striking effects on processes as diverse as arterial pressure regulation, exercise performance, and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data showing impaired hypoxic ventilatory response in TH-HIF-2αKO mice.

claim: Loss of glomus cells has striking effects on arterial pressure regulation.
source: The loss of these cells renders mice incapable of ventilatory responses to hypoxia, and this has striking effects on processes as diverse as arterial pressure regulation, exercise performance, and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by radiotelemetry data showing hypotension in TH-HIF-2αKO mice.

claim: Loss of glomus cells has striking effects on exercise performance.
source: The loss of these cells renders mice incapable of ventilatory responses to hypoxia, and this has striking effects on processes as diverse as arterial pressure regulation, exercise performance, and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced aerobic capacity and power output in TH-HIF-2αKO mice during maximal exertion testing.

claim: Loss of glomus cells has striking effects on glucose homeostasis.
source: The loss of these cells renders mice incapable of ventilatory responses to hypoxia, and this has striking effects on processes as diverse as arterial pressure regulation, exercise performance, and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data showing altered glucose clearance in TH-HIF-2αKO mice.

claim: The expansion of the glomus cells is correlated with mTORC1 activation.
source: We show that the expansion of the glomus cells is correlated with mTORC1 activation, and is functionally inhibited by rapamycin treatment.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased p-S6 staining (mTORC1 activation marker) in glomus cells during hypoxia and reduced p-S6 in HIF-2α deficient embryonic glomus cells.

claim: Glomus cell expansion is functionally inhibited by rapamycin treatment.
source: We show that the expansion of the glomus cells is correlated with mTORC1 activation, and is functionally inhibited by rapamycin treatment.
evidence: Supported by data showing decreased CB volume, TH+ cell numbers, and BrdU+ TH+ cells in rapamycin-treated mice exposed to hypoxia.

claim: The carotid body is located at the carotid artery bifurcation.
source: The carotid body is located at the carotid artery bifurcation, and contains glomeruli that contain O2-sensitive, neuron-like tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive glomus cells (type I cells).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the carotid body location.

claim: The carotid body contains glomeruli that contain O2-sensitive, neuron-like tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive glomus cells (type I cells).
source: The carotid body is located at the carotid artery bifurcation, and contains glomeruli that contain O2-sensitive, neuron-like tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive glomus cells (type I cells).
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotid body cellular composition, supported by citations.

claim: Glomus cells are responsible for a rapid compensatory hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) when a drop in arterial O2 tension (PO2) occurs.
source: These glomus cells are responsible for a rapid compensatory hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) when a drop in arterial O2 tension (PO2) occurs (López-Barneo et al., 2016b; Teppema and Dahan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CB plays an important role in acclimatization to sustained hypoxia.
source: In addition to this acute reflex, the CB plays an important role in acclimatization to sustained hypoxia, and is commonly enlarged in people living at high altitude (Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Wang and Bisgard, 2002) and in patients with chronic respiratory diseases (Heath and Edwards, 1971; Heath et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CB is commonly enlarged in people living at high altitude.
source: In addition to this acute reflex, the CB plays an important role in acclimatization to sustained hypoxia, and is commonly enlarged in people living at high altitude (Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Wang and Bisgard, 2002) and in patients with chronic respiratory diseases (Heath and Edwards, 1971; Heath et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CB is commonly enlarged in patients with chronic respiratory diseases.
source: In addition to this acute reflex, the CB plays an important role in acclimatization to sustained hypoxia, and is commonly enlarged in people living at high altitude (Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Wang and Bisgard, 2002) and in patients with chronic respiratory diseases (Heath and Edwards, 1971; Heath et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CB enlargement is induced through a proliferative response of CB stem cells (type II cells).
source: This enlargement is induced through a proliferative response of CB stem cells (type II cells)(Pardal et al., 2007; Platero-Luengo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During embryogenesis, the initiating event in CB organogenesis occurs when multipotent neural crest cells migrate toward the dorsal aorta, to give rise to the sympathoadrenal system.
source: During embryogenesis, the initiating event in CB organogenesis occurs when multipotent neural crest cells migrate toward the dorsal aorta, to give rise to the sympathoadrenal system (Le Douarin, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Segregation of sympathetic progenitors from the superior cervical ganglion (SCG) creates the CB parenchyma.
source: Segregation of sympathetic progenitors from the superior cervical ganglion (SCG) then creates the CB parenchyma (Kameda, 2005; Kameda et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CB structure is comprised of O2-sensitive glomus cells (type-I cells), glia-like sustentacular cells (type-II cells) and endothelial cells.
source: This structure is comprised of O2-sensitive glomus cells (type-I cells) (Pearse et al., 1973), glia-like sustentacular cells (type-II cells) (Pardal et al., 2007) and endothelial cells (Annese et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mouse models hemizygous for HIFs-α (Hif1a+/- and Epas1+/-) or where HIF inactivation was induced in adults showed contrasting effects on CB function, without in either case affecting CB development.
source: At the organismal level, mouse models hemizygous for HIFs-α (Hif1a+/- and Epas1+/-) or where HIF inactivation was induced in adults showed contrasting effects on CB function, without in either case affecting CB development (Hodson et al., 2016; Kline et al., 2002; Peng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Epas1 (not Hif1a) inactivation had major effects on the proliferative response of the CBs to protracted hypoxia.
source: Nevertheless, in both settings Epas1 (not Hif1a) inactivation, had major effects on the proliferative response of the CBs to protracted hypoxia (Hodson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Epas1 is the second most abundant transcript in neonatal CB glomus cells.
source: Transcriptome analysis has confirmed that Epas1 is the second most abundant transcript in neonatal CB glomus cells (Tian et al., 1998; Zhou et al., 2016), and that it is expressed at far higher levels than are found in cells of similar developmental origins, including superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic neurons (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to transcriptome analysis studies.

claim: Epas1 is expressed at far higher levels in CB glomus cells than are found in cells of similar developmental origins, including superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic neurons.
source: Transcriptome analysis has confirmed that Epas1 is the second most abundant transcript in neonatal CB glomus cells (Tian et al., 1998; Zhou et al., 2016), and that it is expressed at far higher levels than are found in cells of similar developmental origins, including superior cervical ganglion (SCG) sympathetic neurons (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Epas1 but not Hif1a overexpression in sympathoadrenal cells leads to enlargement of the CB.
source: It has also been recently shown that Epas1 but not Hif1a, overexpression in sympathoadrenal cells leads to enlargement of the CB (Macías et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: TH-HIF-2αKO mice have virtually no CB TH+ glomus cells in adults (8-12 weeks old).
source: Histological analysis of the carotid artery bifurcation dissected from adult (8–12 weeks old) TH-HIF-2αKO mice revealed virtually no CB TH+ glomus cells (Figure 1A, bottom panels) compared to HIF-2αWT littermate controls (Figure 1A, top panels).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 1.

claim: TH-HIF-1αKO mice showed a typical glomus cell organization similar to HIF-1αWT littermate controls.
source: Conversely, TH-HIF-1αKO mice showed a typical glomus cell organization, characterized by scattered clusters of TH+ cells throughout the CB parenchyma (Figure 1B, bottom panels) similar to those found in HIF-1αWT littermate controls (Figure 1B, top panels).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Other catecholaminergic organs whose embryological origins are similar to those of the CB, for example, the superior cervical ganglion (SCG), do not show significant differences in structure or volume between TH-HIF-2αKO mutants and control mice.
source: Other catecholaminergic organs whose embryological origins are similar to those of the CB, for example, the superior cervical ganglion (SCG), do not show significant differences in structure or volume between TH-HIF-2αKO mutants and control mice (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 1.

claim: HIF-2α has a specific role in the development of the CB glomus cells, and not a global role in late development of catecholaminergic tissues.
source: This suggests a specific role of HIF-2α in the development of the CB glomus cells, and argues against a global role for the gene in late development of catecholaminergic tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SCG and adrenal medulla are unaffected while CB glomus cells are lost.

claim: No major histological alterations were observed in adrenal glands removed from TH-HIF-2αKO and TH-HIF-1αKO mutant mice compared to HIF-2αWT and HIF-1αWT littermate controls.
source: No major histological alterations were observed in adrenal glands removed from TH-HIF-2αKO and TH-HIF-1αKO mutant mice compared to HIF-2αWT and HIF-1αWT littermate controls (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The amount of catecholamine (adrenaline and noradrenaline) present in the urine of TH-HIF-2αKO and TH-HIF-1αKO deficient mice was similar to that found in their respective littermate controls.
source: Consistent with this, the amount of catecholamine (adrenaline and noradrenaline) present in the urine of TH-HIF-2αKO and TH-HIF-1αKO deficient mice was similar to that found in their respective littermate controls (Figure 1I).
evidence: Demonstrated by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Differentiated TH+ glomus cells were found in the carotid bifurcation of TH-HIF-2αKO mutant mice at embryonic stage E18.5 and postnatally (P0).
source: Differentiated TH+ glomus cells were found in the carotid bifurcation of TH-HIF-2αKO mutant mice at both stages (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the total CB parenchyma volume and in the number of differentiated TH+ glomus cells in TH-HIF-2αKO mice at E18.5, and this reduction is even more evident in newborn mice.
source: However, there is a significant reduction in the total CB parenchyma volume and in the number of differentiated TH+ glomus cells in TH-HIF-2αKO mice at E18.5, and this reduction is even more evident in newborn mice (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative histological analysis shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: There is a progressive increase in the number of TUNEL+ cells within the CB parenchyma of TH-HIF-2αKO mice compared to HIF-2αWT littermates.
source: We next assessed cell death in the developing CB, and found a progressive increase in the number of TUNEL+ cells within the CB parenchyma of TH-HIF-2αKO mice compared to HIF-2αWT littermates (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: HIF-2α, but not HIF-1α, is essential for the survival of CB glomus cells.
source: These data demonstrate that HIF-2α, but not HIF-1α, is essential for the survival of CB glomus cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the developmental data showing loss of glomus cells and increased cell death in TH-HIF-2αKO but not TH-HIF-1αKO mice.

claim: HIF-2αWT mice breathing 10% O2 had a biphasic response, characterized by an initial rapid increase in respiratory rate followed by a slow decline.
source: HIF-2αWT mice breathing 10% O2 had a biphasic response, characterized by an initial rapid increase in respiratory rate followed by a slow decline.
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TH-HIF-2αKO mice, which have normal ventilation rates in normoxia, respond abnormally throughout the hypoxic period.
source: In contrast, TH-HIF-2αKO mice, which have normal ventilation rates in normoxia (Figure 3A–C), respond abnormally throughout the hypoxic period.
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Averaged respiratory rate and minute volume during the initial 5 min of hypoxia show a substantial reduction in ventilation rate in TH-HIF-2αKO mutant mice relative to HIF-2αWT controls.
source: Averaged respiratory rate and minute volume during the initial 5 min of hypoxia show a substantial reduction in ventilation rate in TH-HIF-2αKO mutant mice relative to HIF-2αWT controls (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The respiratory response to hypercapnia (5% CO2) was preserved in TH-HIF-2αKO mice, indicating normal function of the respiratory center.
source: However, the respiratory response to hypercapnia (5% CO2) was preserved in TH-HIF-2αKO mice, indicating normal function of the respiratory center (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Hemoglobin saturation levels dropped to 50–55% in TH-HIF-2αKO mice, as compared to 73% saturation in control animals after exposure to 10% O2 for 5 min.
source: Consistent with a failed HVR, hemoglobin saturation levels dropped to 50–55% in TH-HIF-2αKO mice, as compared to 73% saturation in control animals after exposure to 10% O2 for 5 min (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse oximetry measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: HIF-1αWT and TH-HIF-1αKO mice have similar respiratory responses to 21% O2 and 10% O2, which indicates that HIF-1α is not required for the CB-mediated ventilatory response to hypoxia.
source: HIF-1αWT and TH-HIF-1αKO mice have similar respiratory responses to 21% O2 and 10% O2, which indicates that HIF-1α is not required for the CB-mediated ventilatory response to hypoxia (Figure 3E–G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography data shown in Figure 3E-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-J.

claim: After exposure to hypoxia, TH-HIF-2αKO mice showed lower VO2 and VCO2 peaks and had a significantly hampered metabolic adaptation to low oxygen.
source: After exposure to hypoxia, however, TH-HIF-2αKO mice showed lower VO2 and VCO2 peaks and had a significantly hampered metabolic adaptation to low oxygen (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolic cage measurements shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: The secretory activity of chromaffin cells under basal conditions and in response to hypoxia, hypercapnia and high (20 mM) extracellular K+ was not changed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to control littermates.
source: The secretory activity of chromaffin cells under basal conditions and in response to hypoxia, hypercapnia and high (20 mM) extracellular K+ was not changed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice (8–12 weeks old) relative to control littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by amperometric recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Current-voltage (I-V) relationships for Ca2+ and K+ currents of dispersed chromaffin cells and SCG neurons were similar in HIF-2αWT and TH-HIF-2αKO animals.
source: Current-voltage (I-V) relationships for Ca2+ and K+ currents of dispersed chromaffin cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) and SCG neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F) were also similar in HIF-2αWT and TH-HIF-2αKO animals.
evidence: Demonstrated by patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: HIF-2α loss in the sympathoadrenal lineages predominantly affects CB glomus cells.
source: These data further support the notion that HIF-2α loss in the sympathoadrenal lineages predominantly affects CB glomus cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that adrenal medulla and SCG function are preserved while CB function is lost.

claim: A normal number of CB GFAP+ stem cells were identified in the carotid artery bifurcation of TH-HIF-2αKO mice.
source: Despite the absence of adult TH+ oxygen sensing cells in TH-HIF-2αKO mice, we identified a normal number of CB GFAP+ stem cells in the carotid artery bifurcation of these animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by GFAP immunostaining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Typical CB enlargement and emergence of double BrdU+ TH+ glomus cells was seen in HIF-2αWT mice after 14 days breathing 10% O2.
source: Typical CB enlargement and emergence of double BrdU+ TH+ glomus cells was seen in HIF-2αWT mice after 14 days breathing 10% O2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D), as previously described (Pardal et al., 2007).
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU labeling and histological analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: No newly formed double BrdU+ TH+ glomus cells were observed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice after 14 days in hypoxia.
source: However, no newly formed double BrdU+ TH+ glomus cells were observed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice after 14 days in hypoxia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by BrdU labeling and histological analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: HIF-2αWT, HIF-1αWT and TH-HIF-1αKO mice adapted well and survived up to 21 days in a 10% O2 atmosphere normally.
source: HIF-2αWT, HIF-1αWT and TH-HIF-1αKO mice adapted well and survived up to 21 days in a 10% O2 atmosphere normally.
evidence: Demonstrated by survival data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Long-term survival of the TH-HIF-2αKO deficient mice kept in a 10% O2 environment was severely compromised, and only 40% reached the experimental endpoint.
source: However, long-term survival of the TH-HIF-2αKO deficient mice kept in a 10% O2 environment was severely compromised, and only 40% reached the experimental endpoint (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival curve shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The right ventricle was found to be significantly enlarged in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to control mice after 21 days of 10% O2 exposure, indicating an aggravation of pulmonary hypertension.
source: The right ventricle was found to be significantly enlarged in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to control mice after 21 days of 10% O2 exposure, indicating an aggravation of pulmonary hypertension (Figure 4H).
evidence: Demonstrated by Fulton index measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The percentage of fully muscularized lung peripheral vessels is significantly increased in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to controls after chronic hypoxia.
source: Lung histology of mice chronically exposed to 10% O2 (Figure 4J) shows that the percentage of fully muscularized lung peripheral vessels is significantly increased in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to controls.
evidence: Demonstrated by lung histology analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The tunica media of lung peripheral vessels was significantly thicker in TH-HIF-2αKO mice compared to HIF-2αWT littermates after 21 days of hypoxic exposure.
source: The tunica media of lung peripheral vessels was also significantly thicker in TH-HIF-2αKO mice compared to HIF-2αWT littermates after 21 days of hypoxic exposure (Figure 4K).
evidence: Demonstrated by lung histology analysis shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Adaptation to chronic hypoxia is highly reliant on a normally functioning CB.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that adaptation to chronic hypoxia is highly reliant on a normally functioning CB.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the severe maladaptation observed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice during chronic hypoxia.

claim: Circadian blood pressure monitoring showed a significantly hypotensive condition in TH-HIF-2αKO mice that was more pronounced during the diurnal period.
source: Circadian blood pressure monitoring showed a significantly hypotensive condition that was more pronounced during the diurnal period (Figure 5A and B) and did not correlate with changes in heart rate, subcutaneous temperature or activity (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by radiotelemetry measurements shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: TH-HIF-2αKO mice failed to recover from hypoxia-induced hypotension, and showed a persistent hypotensive state throughout the hypoxic period.
source: However, while TH-HIF-2αKO mice experienced similar, but less deep, hypotension 3 hr post hypoxic challenge, they failed to recover, and showed a persistent hypotensive state throughout the hypoxic period (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by radiotelemetry measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The bradycardic effect of hypoxia on heart rate was abolished in TH-HIF-2αKO animals.
source: Interestingly, the bradycardic effect of hypoxia on heart rate was abolished in TH-HIF-2αKO animals (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by radiotelemetry measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The CB is a systemic cardiovascular regulator which contributes to baseline blood pressure modulation, is critical for cardiovascular adaptations to hypoxia and delays the development of Ang II-induced experimental hypertension.
source: Collectively, these data highlight the CB as a systemic cardiovascular regulator which, contributes to baseline blood pressure modulation, is critical for cardiovascular adaptations to hypoxia and delays the development of Ang II-induced experimental hypertension.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cardiovascular phenotypes observed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice.

claim: TH-HIF-2αKO mutants reached VO2max much earlier than wild type controls, with significantly decreased heat generation.
source: However, TH-HIF-2αKO mutants reached VO2max much earlier than wild type controls, with significantly decreased heat generation (Figure 6A,B and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by metabolic measurements during exercise testing shown in Figure 6A, B, and D.

claim: There was a significant reduction in both aerobic capacity and power output in TH-HIF-2αKO mice relative to littermate controls during exercise.
source: There was a significant reduction in both aerobic capacity and power output relative to littermate controls (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by exercise testing measurements shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: TH-HIF-2αKO mice showed an initially hampered lactate clearance relative to control mice.
source: TH-HIF-2αKO mice also showed an initially hampered lactate clearance relative to control mice (Figure 6N).
evidence: Demonstrated by lactate tolerance test shown in Figure 6N.

claim: The CB plays a role in metabolic adaptations triggered by both exercise and hyperglycemia.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the mutants demonstrate intriguing roles for the CB in metabolic adaptations triggered by both exercise and hyperglycemia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the metabolic phenotypes observed in TH-HIF-2αKO mice during exercise and glucose challenge.

claim: After 14 days in a 10% O2 environment, there was a significantly increased p-S6 signal within the CB TH+ cells while the SCG sympathetic neurons remained at levels similar to those seen in normoxia.
source: However, after 14 days in a 10% O2 environment, we saw a significantly increased p-S6 signal within the CB TH+ cells while the SCG sympathetic neurons remained at levels similar to those seen in normoxia (Figure 7A and B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: In E18.5 embryos there was a striking accumulation of p-S6; this is significantly reduced in HIF-2α deficient CB TH+ cells in embryos from this stage of development.
source: In E18.5 embryos there was a striking accumulation of p-S6; this is significantly reduced in HIF-2α deficient CB TH+ cells in embryos from this stage of development (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: HIF-2α regulates mTORC1 activity in the CB glomus cells during development.
source: These data indicate that HIF-2α regulates mTORC1 activity in the CB glomus cells during development.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that p-S6 levels are reduced in HIF-2α deficient embryonic CB glomus cells.

claim: Histological analysis of rapamycin injected wild type mice maintained for 14 days at 10% O2 showed decreased CB parenchyma volume, TH+ cells number, and showed a dramatic reduction in the number of proliferating double BrdU+ TH+ cells when compared to vehicle-injected mice.
source: Interestingly, histological analysis of rapamycin injected wild type mice maintained for 14 days at 10% O2 showed decreased CB parenchyma volume, TH+ cells number, and showed a dramatic reduction in the number of proliferating double BrdU+ TH+ cells when compared to vehicle-injected mice (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: Rapamycin treated mice had a decreased VAH compared to vehicle-injected control mice following 7 days at 10% O2.
source: Consistent with the histological analysis above, rapamycin treated mice had a decreased VAH compared to vehicle-injected control mice following 7 days at 10% O2 (Figure 7I).
evidence: Demonstrated by plethysmography measurements shown in Figure 7I.

claim: mTORC1 activation is required for CB glomus cell development, in a HIF-2α-dependent manner.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that mTORC1 activation is required for CB glomus cell development, in a HIF-2α-dependent manner, and that this activation regulates CB growth as well as VAH during prolonged hypoxia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined observations of reduced mTORC1 activity in HIF-2α deficient CB and the effects of rapamycin on CB proliferation.

claim: mTORC1 activation regulates CB growth as well as VAH during prolonged hypoxia.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that mTORC1 activation is required for CB glomus cell development, in a HIF-2α-dependent manner, and that this activation regulates CB growth as well as VAH during prolonged hypoxia.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the effects of rapamycin on CB proliferation and ventilatory acclimatization.

claim: Embryological deletion of Epas1, but not Hif1a, specifically in sympathoadrenal tissues (TH+) prevents O2-sensitive glomus cell development, without affecting SCG sympathetic neurons or AM chromaffin cells of the same embryological origin.
source: However, our findings demonstrate that embryological deletion of Epas1, but not Hif1a, specifically in sympathoadrenal tissues (TH+) prevents O2-sensitive glomus cell development, without affecting SCG sympathetic neurons or AM chromaffin cells of the same embryological origin.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by histological and functional data.

claim: The specific role of HIF-2α in CB glomus cell development is not due to a generalized effect on late development of the sympathoadrenal system.
source: Therefore, these results highlight the specific role of HIF-2α in CB glomus cell development, rather than a generalized effect on late development of the sympathoadrenal system.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that other sympathoadrenal tissues are unaffected.

claim: Either over-expression or deficiency of HIF-2α clearly perturbs CB development and, by extension, function.
source: Thus either over-expression or deficiency of HIF-2α clearly perturbs CB development and, by extension, function.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the current study and previous studies showing CB enlargement with HIF-2α overexpression.

claim: Environmental hypoxia can trigger growth of specialized tissues, including the CB and the pulmonary arteries.
source: However, environmental hypoxia can also trigger growth of a number of specialized tissues, including the CB (Arias-Stella and Valcarcel, 1976; Pardal et al., 2007) and the pulmonary arteries (Madden et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the context of hypoxia-induced tissue growth, the HIF-2α isoform seems to play the more prominent role.
source: In this context, the HIF-2α isoform seems to play the more prominent role, and has been associated with pulmonary vascular remodeling as well as with bronchial epithelial proliferation (Brusselmans et al., 2003; Bryant et al., 2016; Cowburn et al., 2016; Kapitsinou et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2013; Torres-Capelli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CB enlargement induced by hypoxia to a large extent recapitulates the cellular events that give rise to mature O2-sensitive glomus cells in development.
source: CB enlargement induced by hypoxia to a large extent recapitulates the cellular events that give rise to mature O2-sensitive glomus cells in development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between developmental and hypoxia-induced CB expansion.

claim: Global HIF-2α, but not HIF-1α, inactivation in adult mice impaired CB growth and associated VAH caused by exposure to chronic hypoxia.
source: In a recent study, global HIF-2α, but not HIF-1α, inactivation in adult mice was shown to impair CB growth and associated VAH caused by exposure to chronic hypoxia (Hodson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: mTORC1 is a central regulator of cellular metabolism, proliferation and survival.
source: Our findings reveal that mTORC1, a central regulator of cellular metabolism, proliferation and survival (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012), is necessary for CB O2-sensitive glomus cell proliferation; and further, that impact in the subsequent enhancement of the hypoxic ventilatory response induced by chronic hypoxia.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: mTORC1 is necessary for CB O2-sensitive glomus cell proliferation and impacts the subsequent enhancement of the hypoxic ventilatory response induced by chronic hypoxia.
source: Our findings reveal that mTORC1, a central regulator of cellular metabolism, proliferation and survival (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012), is necessary for CB O2-sensitive glomus cell proliferation; and further, that impact in the subsequent enhancement of the hypoxic ventilatory response induced by chronic hypoxia.
evidence: Demonstrated by rapamycin experiments showing reduced CB proliferation and VAH.

claim: mTORC1 activity is reduced in HIF-2α-deficient embryonic glomus cells, but not in SCG sympathetic neurons.
source: Importantly, we found that mTORC1 activity is reduced in HIF-2α-deficient embryonic glomus cells, but not in SCG sympathetic neurons, which likely explains the absence of a functional adult CB in these mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by p-S6 immunofluorescence analysis in embryonic tissues.

claim: The activity of mTORC1 may be repressed via HIF-1α-induced gene expression of Ddit4 or Bnip3.
source: For instance, the activity of mTORC1 may be repressed via HIF-1α-induced gene expression of Ddit4 or Bnip3 (Brugarolas et al., 2004; Li et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HIF-2α regulates mTORC1 activity in VHL-deficient tumour cells through the transcriptional control of the amino acid transporter Slc7a5.
source: On the other hand, it has been shown that HIF-2α regulates mTORC1 activity in VHL-deficient tumour cells through the transcriptional control of the amino acid transporter Slc7a5 (Elorza et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Both somatic and germline EPAS1 gain-of-function mutations have been found in patients with paraganglioma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of neural crest origin.
source: As HIF-2α regulates mTORC1 activity to promote proliferation, this connection could prove relevant in pathological situations; for example, both somatic and germline EPAS1 gain-of-function mutations have been found in patients with paraganglioma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of neural crest origin (Lorenzo et al., 2013; Zhuang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CB tumors are 10 times more frequent in people living at high altitude.
source: Indeed, CB tumors are 10 times more frequent in people living at high altitude (Saldana et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The mTOR pathway is commonly activated in both paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma tumors.
source: As further evidence of this link, it has been shown that the mTOR pathway is commonly activated in both paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma tumors (Du et al., 2016; Favier et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mice lacking CB O2-sensitive cells (TH-HIF-2αKO mice) have impaired respiratory, cardiovascular and metabolic adaptive responses.
source: Our data show that mice lacking CB O2-sensitive cells (TH-HIF-2αKO mice) have impaired respiratory, cardiovascular and metabolic adaptive responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings demonstrated by various experimental approaches.

claim: Hemizygous Epas1+/- mice showed different effects compared to TH-HIF-2αKO mice, which might be explained by the complete CB loss of function in TH-HIF-2αKO mice.
source: Although previous studies have linked HIF-2α and CB function (Hodson et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2011), none of them exhibited a complete CB loss of function. This might explain the differing effects observed in hemizygous Epas1+/- mice (Hodson et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2011) compared to our TH-HIF-2αKO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the current study with previous studies.

claim: Hemizygous Hif1a+/- mice exhibited a normal acute HVR.
source: Consistent with this, hemizygous Hif1a+/- mice exhibited a normal acute HVR (Hodson et al., 2016; Kline et al., 2002) albeit some otherwise aberrant CB activities in response to hypoxia (Kline et al., 2002; Ortega-Sáenz et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alterations in CB development and/or function have been associated with diseases such as heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sudden death infant syndrome and hypertension.
source: Alterations in CB development and/or function have recently acquired increasing potential clinical significance and have been associated with diseases such as heart failure, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sudden death infant syndrome and hypertension (Iturriaga et al., 2016; López-Barneo et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This is the first mouse model with specific loss of carotid body O2-sensitive cells that is viable in normoxia but shows impaired physiological adaptations to both acute and chronic hypoxia.
source: We describe here the first mouse model with specific loss of carotid body O2-sensitive cells: a model that is viable in normoxia but shows impaired physiological adaptations to both acute and chronic hypoxia.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main contribution of the study.

claim: The CB has new and likely important roles in systemic blood pressure regulation, exercise performance and glucose management.
source: In addition, we describe new and likely important roles for the CB in systemic blood pressure regulation, exercise performance and glucose management (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of novel findings from the study.
